title: useRef
subtitle: DOM access and mutable values that don't trigger re-renders
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Two needs: (1) Imperatively accessing a DOM element (focus an input, measure an element's size, play a video) without React controlling it through state. (2) Storing a value that persists across renders but doesn't need to cause a re-render when it changes (a timer ID, a previous value, an instance variable).
whyItExists.solution: useRef returns a mutable object { current: initialValue }. React doesn't watch .current — changing it never triggers a re-render. Attach a ref to a DOM element with the ref prop and React will set .current to the DOM node after render.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Focus management, scroll into view, measure element dimensions, integrate third-party libraries that need a DOM node. Storing mutable values like timer IDs, previous state, or flags without causing re-renders.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't use refs to store state that should drive the UI — use useState for that. Don't read or write a ref during render (it can cause inconsistency with React's model). Don't use refs to work around missing useEffect dependencies.

explainModes.beginner: useRef gives you a 'box' you can put any value in. When you attach it to a DOM element with ref={myRef}, React fills the box with the actual DOM element. You can then call myRef.current.focus() or myRef.current.scrollIntoView(). Changing the box's value doesn't re-render the component.
explainModes.simple: const ref = useRef(initialValue). ref.current is the stored value. For DOM refs: <input ref={ref} /> — after mount, ref.current is the input element. Changing ref.current never triggers a re-render. Common uses: focus on mount (useEffect(() => { ref.current?.focus(); }, [])), previous value (store previous state in a ref, update in useEffect after render), cancel tokens (store interval/timeout IDs).
explainModes.standard: Ref vs state: both persist across renders. State change → re-render. Ref change → no re-render. Use state for values that should update the UI; use ref for values that should not. callback refs: instead of useRef, pass a function as the ref prop: ref={node => { if (node) node.focus(); }}. This is called each time the element is added/removed. React.forwardRef: lets a component receive a ref from its parent — essential for custom input components.
explainModes.technical: useRef(null) vs useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null) in TypeScript: the generic specifies the type of the DOM element, giving you type-safe .current properties (focus, value, etc.). The ref object identity is stable — it's the same object every render. This is why it's safe to include in useEffect without causing extra re-runs. useImperativeHandle: used with forwardRef to expose a limited API from a component, rather than the full DOM node.
explainModes.deepDive: Ref forwarding pattern: <TextInput ref={inputRef} /> — the parent holds the ref, the TextInput implementation decides which DOM node to expose. Without forwardRef, ref would be swallowed. The pattern: const TextInput = React.forwardRef((props, ref) => <input {...props} ref={ref} />). React 19 simplifies this: ref becomes a regular prop, so forwardRef wrapping won't be needed. Ref as escape hatch: refs are for escaping React's declarative model for imperative code. They're useful for focus, animation (third-party), video/audio control, and canvas operations. Overusing refs is a smell — most problems are solvable declaratively.

questions.question: When you change `ref.current`, does React re-render the component?
options: Yes — React watches all ref values and re-renders when they change
No — changing ref.current is silent; React is unaware of the change and will NOT re-render
Only if the ref is attached to a DOM element
Yes, but only in development mode
questions.explanation: Refs are intentionally 'outside' React's reactive system. Changing ref.current does not notify React and does not trigger a re-render. This is what makes refs useful for storing values like timer IDs — you can update them without causing unnecessary renders. For values that should update the UI, use state instead.

faq.q: When should I use useRef vs useState?
faq.a: Use useState when the value should cause the UI to update when it changes. Use useRef when the value should persist across renders but NOT cause a re-render: timer IDs, DOM nodes, previous values, flags. Rule of thumb: if you'd ever display the value in JSX, it's state. If it's purely for internal bookkeeping or DOM access, it's a ref.
